title: Deaths in Detention: Mortality Rate for People Detained by ICE More Than Doubles Under Trump Administration
summary: Death rate could be higher if it includes hidden deaths of people released from detention that ICE is reporting under Trump administration.

# Deaths in Detention: Mortality Rate for People Detained by ICE More Than Doubles Under Trump Administration


Due to recent cuts to reporting requirements of deaths occurring after release, the complete number of deaths in and outside of detention could be even higher.


[Sofia Gonzalez](https://www.aclu.org/bios/sofia-gonzalez) ,
National Prison Project


**Share This Page**


September 22, 2026


While detained at Stewart Detention Center in Georgia,[Prisciliano Trejo Ricano](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/the-deaths-ice-doesnt-count/) experienced severe symptoms, including coughing up blood and severe pain. After weeks struggling to access medical care, he was transferred to a nearby hospital. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) formally released him from custody when he was in a coma. He died from an aggressive form of leukemia less than two weeks later.


Trejo Ricano’s name does not appear on the ICE website as one of the people who died while in ICE custody, and ICE will not be investigating what led to his death so shortly after being released from Stewart due to recent policy changes.


The mortality rate for people in ICE custody has[more than doubled](https://www.hrw.org/report/2026/06/25/dying-in-detention/rising-deaths-in-an-expanding-us-immigration-detention-system) from the first Trump administration and is at its highest point in more than a decade. At least 57 people have died in immigration detention since the start of the second term, more than double the number of deaths recorded from the previous four years combined. As egregious as the current mortality rate is, it still does not include an accurate death toll resulting from the neglect in ICE detention centers because of hidden deaths like Trejo Ricano’s.


## Trump administration removes crucial deaths reporting requirements


Beyond recorded in-custody deaths, ICE has hidden a growing number of fatalities due to recent shifts in reporting mandates. In 2021, the Department of Homeland Security implemented a federal policy requiring ICE to report and[investigate any deaths](https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/policy/11003.5_NotifRevReportReqDetaineeDeaths.pdf) occurring within 30 days of release from ICE custody. This measure ensured that[ICE could be held accountable](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/05/ice-deaths-data-memo) and prevented it from releasing severely ill individuals to dodge accountability and reporting requirements. The Trump administration rescinded that policy in June in yet another move to evade oversight and transparency.


By eliminating these reporting requirements, ICE shields itself from accountability for the human cost of its medical failures. ICE is then incentivized to discharge critically ill individuals just before they die, artificially skewing official mortality statistics. Ultimately, erasing these accountability metrics only emboldens the agency to continue operating with minimal transparency, leaving detained immigrants even more vulnerable to systemic neglect and abuse.


Despite federal efforts to obstruct meaningful oversight and obscure these fatalities, the ACLU remains dedicated to exposing the full extent of hidden deaths in ICE custody. Through targeted Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and litigation, we are fighting to ensure the deaths of these individuals are tracked so that ICE is held accountable for the true cost of its detention conditions.

### The People v. Agents of Chaos and Cruelty


In 2022, we submitted our first FOIA request seeking more information about ICE’s pattern of deathbed releases. This request sought documents related to four deaths, along with additional documents that would lead to more information about ICE’s policies and practices around these deaths and potentially uncover additional unreported deaths. When the government failed to respond to this FOIA request, we filed a lawsuit to obtain responsive documents. After successfully obtaining some records, the ACLU submitted another FOIA request for similar information in July this year. In addition to requesting records related to certain deathbed releases, that FOIA request also asks for documents relating to the latest elimination of the requirement for ICE to report and investigate the deaths of those people who die shortly after being released from detention. The ACLU is committed to shed light on these hidden deaths. That transparency is critical if we are to achieve the radical reform to put a stop to the alarming rise in deaths connected to ICE detention.


## Limited oversight and egregious conditions persist in ICE detention


On any given day, ICE holds[approximately 70,000 people](https://deportationdata.org/) across a sprawling network of over[200 immigration detention centers.](https://detentionreports.com/) As rates of immigration detention rise, the rate of deaths in detention has also surged to unprecedented levels. With the[rapid proliferation of new detention centers](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/deaths-in-detention-ice-is-rapidly-expanding-detention-camps-into-warehouses-despite-record-deaths) in the form of warehouses and shuttered prisons and expansion of detention beds in existing facilities, this rising death toll raises urgent questions about proper access to healthcare, hygiene and nutrition, and conditions of confinement more broadly.

### Deaths in Detention: ICE Is Rapidly Expanding Detention Camps into Warehouses Despite Record Deaths


Despite a record number of deaths in ICE detention, Trump is doubling down on his mass detention and deportation campaign by buying warehouses to…


**By:** Haddy Gassama


Explore news & commentary


[Deaths In Detention: Ice Is Rapidly Expanding Detention Camps Into Warehouses Despite Record Deaths. Explore News & Commentary.](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/deaths-in-detention-ice-is-rapidly-expanding-detention-camps-into-warehouses-despite-record-deaths)


News & Commentary


Apr 2026


Immigrants' Rights


Human Rights


**By:** Haddy Gassama


Alongside the rapid growth of detention operations, the administration has systemically dismantled key internal oversight mechanisms within DHS. The limited oversight mechanisms that were in place to ensure accountability in immigration detention, including the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman and the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, have been[effectively gutted](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-homeland-department-targets-oversight-government-cuts-2025-03-21/) , shutting down essential avenues for public complaints and accountability.


“These offices have obstructed immigration enforcement by adding bureaucratic hurdles and undermining DHS’s mission,”[a DHS spokesperson](https://www.npr.org/2025/03/21/nx-s1-5336738/homeland-security-rif-cuts-dhs) said in defense of the cuts. “Rather than supporting law enforcement efforts, they often function as internal adversaries that slow down operations.” By stripping away internal checks and balances, DHS has created a vacuum of oversight, furthering concerns that officers are now empowered to operate in the shadows.


Compounding with this lack of oversight, the rapid expansion of detention facilities has further strained already problematic ICE operations. The agency is consistently failing to meet basic human needs, subjecting tens of thousands of people every day to systemic and dangerous medical neglect, unacceptable sanitation conditions, and unsafe housing. For many, these dire conditions have resulted in[preventable medical crises and fatalities](https://phr.org/our-work/resources/dying-in-detention/) . Without radical systemic reform and restored oversight, the current number of deaths in and outside of detention will almost certainly continue to climb.


The ACLU obtained this data from[ICE’s detainee death reports](https://www.ice.gov/detain/detainee-death-reporting) from 2018 to 2026 and the[Texas Standard](https://texasstandard.org/stories/in-2017-the-number-of-immigrants-who-died-in-ice-detention-centers-reached-an-eight-year-high/) for 2017 data.


Environmental and operational conditions inside detention facilities directly contribute to the surge in rising deaths. Overcrowding and staffing shortages create[dangerous conditions](https://www.aclu.org/documents/report-of-the-external-monitor-on-medical-care-at-california-city-detention-facility) for people in detention. Unsanitary conditions mean that disease runs rampant, and several facilities have reported outbreaks of[measles](https://apnews.com/article/camp-east-montana-immigration-detention-measles-7c70b887234439f96af405f2f16953c9) and[tuberculosis](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/14/tuberculosis-outbreak-colorado-ice-jail) that have triggered multi-week quarantines. For those with preexisting medical or mental health conditions, slow response times and inadequate care can turn manageable illnesses into life threatening emergencies. In addition to medical neglect,[reports document](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/report-finds-deaths-neglect-in-fort-bliss-immigration-detention) rampant physical abuse, excessive force, and solitary confinement. These egregious and inhumane conditions coerce people into abandoning their immigration and asylum claims and signing voluntary departure orders to[third countries](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/the-trump-administration-is-disappearing-immigrants-and-asylum-seekers-in-growing-third-country-removal-campaign) .


Facing increased scrutiny, DHS has also recently announced a pause on the purchase of additional warehouses for immigration detention. Still, some of the facilities the agency has already acquired will continue to be developed for mass detention. Amid record deaths, documented abuses, and signs of profit-seeking, the expansion of immigration detention facilities demands urgent action. We encourage members of the[House](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6397) and[Senate](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/1208) to co-sponsor the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act. The bill would repeal mandatory detention, end family detention, and create a presumption of release and impose a higher burden of proof to detain primary caregivers and vulnerable populations. It would also phase out the use of private detention facilities and jails over a three-year period and require DHS to establish civil detention standards that provide, at minimum, the level of protection in the American Bar Association’s Civil Immigration Detention Standards. The bill would also mandate the DHS inspector general to conduct unannounced inspections with meaningful penalties for failure to comply with standards and require DHS to admit members of congress to detention facilities for unannounced inspections. The question is no longer whether the system is broken, but whether we are willing to confront and dismantle what it has become.

### Immigrants’ Rights Organizations File Lawsuit to Stop ICE from Hiding Locations of Detained People


BOSTON — A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers. The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients. For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification. The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported. The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds. The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law. The following are statements from the plaintiffs and their legal counsel: Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.” Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.” Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.” Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?” Aimee Mayer-Salins, deputy program director of legal coordination at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights: “When someone you love is in ICE custody, they shouldn’t simply disappear into a black hole. Families deserve to know where their loved ones are being held, and this lawsuit is about protecting that basic right.” For more information about Greater Boston Legal Services et al. v. Mullin, visit: https://www.aclu.org/cases/greater-boston-legal-services-et-al-v-mullin


**Court Case:** Greater Boston Legal Services et al. v. Mullin

### New ACLU Film Exposes Human Toll of Immigration Raid in Wilder, Idaho as Families’ Lawsuit Moves Forward


NEW YORK – The American Civil Liberties Union premiered Wilder Raids, an original short film telling the story of two families whose lives were upended by a violent immigration raid at a horse-racing event in Wilder, Idaho, one year ago today. The film follows the families as they reckon with the lasting trauma of the raid and details the ongoing lawsuit brought by the ACLU, ACLU of Idaho, Cooley LLP, and Stoel Rives LLP seeking accountability. One year ago today, more than 200 federal, state, and local law enforcement officers descended on an otherwise peaceful family event at a horse-racing track in Wilder, Idaho. Law enforcement arrived in armored trucks and a helicopter with flashbang grenades and guns drawn and detained approximately 400 spectators – including U.S. citizens and children – for four hours in inhumane conditions before subjecting everyone to suspicionless immigration interrogations. Through interviews with the families and an inside look at the ongoing legal fight, Wilder Raids explores the lasting impact of the raid on those who experienced it and the broader Wilder community. Juana Rodriguez, one of the lead plaintiffs and featured storyteller in the film, is a U.S. citizen who was at the event with her 3-year-old son. After being violently rounded up with hundreds of other families, Rodriguez was placed in zip ties and detained for several hours without food or water. Law enforcement instructed her toddler to hold onto her pocket while Rodriguez remained zip tied and unable to comfort her son. “I was like, why? I have my son with me. I have to take care of him. I was scared. If I overreacted, I felt like they were going to hurt me,” Rodriguez said. “For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water … I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn’t. I think that’s what really gets to me till this day.” The families featured in the film filed a lawsuit last February that argues that federal, state, and local law enforcement used criminal warrants as a pretext for a sweeping immigration dragnet at an event where they knew attendees would be predominantly Latino. The complaint further alleges that the agencies conspired to deprive those detained of their Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable seizures and their right to equal protection regardless of ethnicity. The lawsuit invokes federal civil rights laws enacted after the Civil War to protect people from racialized government violence and provides a potential avenue for holding federal actors accountable for constitutional violations. “Defendants continue to characterize what happened in Wilder as an ordinary warrant execution, but there was nothing routine about the terror they inflicted on hundreds of people trying to spend a Sunday with their families,” said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU. “This film makes it impossible to ignore what our clients and their families experienced that day and puts a human face on the reckless violence and cruelty inflicted on the community. One year later, we will not let the government rewrite what happened in Wilder and we will continue fighting to hold those responsible accountable.” “The violent raid in Wilder has had significant ripple effects across many communities in Idaho, which can still be felt today, a year later,” said Leo Morales, executive director of the ACLU of Idaho. “The film reminds us of how critical it is for every American to rise to the challenge of protecting civil liberties. It also highlights how personal and fragile our rights can be if left unprotected from government action. Families cannot simply shake off and ignore the abuse; it is our collective responsibility to seek justice, take action, and make things whole.” The lawsuit is ongoing as the families await a decision on the defendants’ motions to dismiss. On Sept. 8, 2026, plaintiffs filed an opposition brief urging the federal court to allow the lawsuit to proceed. Additional statements from co-counsel are below. Jade Ford, an attorney at Cooley LLP: “This film sends a clear message: the Wilder community will not stand idly by in the face of constitutional violations. Every person in this country is entitled to freedom from unlawful seizure and freedom from discriminatory targeting. Those are not hollow promises—they are vital constitutional guarantees, and the Wilder community intends to see them enforced.” Wendy Olsen, an attorney at Stoel Rives LLP: “All Idaho families should be able to enjoy community and cultural events without fear that their rights will be violated, that their children will be traumatized or that they will be targeted based on their perceived color or national origin. This film bravely tells that story on behalf of the Wilder community.”


**Court Case:** Rodriguez, et al. v. Porter, et al.
